people.name: Tiberius Gracchus
people.summary: Grandson of Scipio Africanus and son of the twice-consul Ti. Sempronius Gracchus, he carried the agrarian law of 133 through the plebeian assembly, deposed a vetoing colleague and was clubbed to death on the Capitol while seeking re-election.
people.detail: As quaestor in 137 he negotiated the treaty that saved Mancinus' army at Numantia, which the senate repudiated, a humiliation some ancient writers saw as his motive. His speeches, quoted by Plutarch and Appian, framed the land question as the plight of soldiers who had 'not a clod of earth to call their own'. Whether a sincere reformer or ambitious noble, he made the tribunate and the popular assembly instruments of policy against the senate.
people.death: clubbed to death on the Capitol by senators led by Scipio Nasica during the tribunician elections, summer 133

people.name: Gaius Gracchus
people.summary: Younger brother of Tiberius and the greatest orator of his generation, he passed a sweeping legislative programme in two tribunates (123-122): subsidised grain, equestrian juries, Asian tax contracts, colonies, roads and protection against summary execution. He died in the first use of the senatus consultum ultimum.
people.detail: Cicero considered him the most gifted orator Rome had produced. A dream in which Tiberius told him he could not escape the same fate was reported by Cicero from Gaius' own account. His laws reshaped Roman politics for a century, binding the equites and urban plebs into politics as distinct interests.
people.death: had his slave Philocrates kill him in the grove of Furrina as Opimius' forces closed in, 121

people.name: Cornelia
people.summary: Daughter of Scipio Africanus and mother of the Gracchi, she bore twelve children of whom three survived, refused a marriage offer from Ptolemy VIII, and became the model Roman matron, famous for calling her sons her jewels.
people.detail: Her statue, set up in the Porticus Metelli, had a base inscribed 'Cornelia, daughter of Africanus, mother of the Gracchi' (CIL VI 31610). Fragments of letters ascribed to her in Cornelius Nepos urge Gaius not to stand for the tribunate; their authenticity is disputed. She retired to Misenum and kept a cultured household.
people.death: natural causes at Misenum, date uncertain (after 121)

people.name: Marcus Octavius
people.summary: Tribune in 133 and friend of Tiberius Gracchus, he vetoed the agrarian bill, himself possessing much public land, and was removed from office by a vote of the plebeian assembly, an unprecedented act.

people.name: Scipio Nasica Serapio
people.summary: Pontifex maximus and leader of the senatorial attack that killed Tiberius Gracchus on the Capitol in 133. Sent to Asia on an embassy to remove him from popular hatred, he died at Pergamon.
people.detail: As consul in 138 he had been briefly imprisoned by tribunes over the levy. His nickname Serapio, from a resemblance to a pig dealer, was given him by a tribune. He was the first pontifex maximus to leave Italy.
people.death: died at Pergamon, 132

people.name: Aristonicus
people.summary: Illegitimate son of Eumenes II, he resisted the Roman inheritance of Pergamon as King Eumenes III, recruiting slaves and the rural poor, defeated and killed the consul Crassus Mucianus, and was captured at Stratonicea by Perperna.
people.death: strangled in prison at Rome, 129 or 128

people.name: Eunus
people.summary: A Syrian slave from Apamea at Enna, a wonder-worker who breathed fire from a nut-shell filled with embers, he led the First Sicilian Slave War, took the royal name Antiochus and minted coins. He was captured after the fall of Henna.
people.death: died in prison at Morgantina, of disease, c. 132

people.name: Opimius

roles.t: Head of the commission dividing Numidia

people.summary: Destroyer of Fregellae as praetor and, as consul in 121, the first magistrate to act under a senatus consultum ultimum, killing Gaius Gracchus and Fulvius Flaccus and executing thousands of their followers. Acquitted in 120, he was condemned in 109 for taking Jugurtha's bribes.
people.detail: The vintage of his consular year, the Opimian wine of 121, became legendary; Pliny says some of it survived, thick as honey, almost two centuries later.
people.death: in exile at Dyrrachium, date unknown

people.name: Fulvius Flaccus
people.summary: Gracchan ally who proposed citizenship for the Italians as consul in 125, conducted the first Roman campaign beyond the Alps for Massalia, and took the extraordinary step for an ex-consul of serving as tribune with Gaius Gracchus in 122.
people.death: killed with his son while hiding in a bath-house after the Aventine was stormed, 121

people.name: Marcus Livius Drusus (tribune 122)
people.summary: Senatorial tribune who outbid Gaius Gracchus in 122 with proposals for twelve colonies and rent-free allotments, splitting Gaius' following. As consul and proconsul he triumphed over the Scordisci in Macedonia. Father of the tribune of 91.
people.death: died during his censorship, 109

people.name: Jugurtha

roles.t: Commander of Numidian contingent at Numantia

people.summary: Grandson of Masinissa and adopted son of Micipsa, he served under Scipio at Numantia, seized all Numidia by murdering his co-heirs, massacred Italian traders at Cirta and fought Rome for seven years, exposing the venality of the Roman nobility. Betrayed by Bocchus to Sulla, he was paraded in Marius' triumph.
people.detail: Sallust portrays him as brilliant, charming and ruthless, a mirror held up to Roman decline. His war made the careers of Marius and Sulla and was the immediate occasion of the enrolment of the capite censi.
people.death: starved to death in the Tullianum at Rome after Marius' triumph, January 104
scholarship: Paul, A Historical Commentary on Sallust's Bellum Jugurthinum (1984)

people.name: Metellus Numidicus
people.summary: Incorruptible aristocrat who restored discipline to the Roman army in Numidia (109-108) and beat Jugurtha at the Muthul, only to be superseded by his own legate Marius. As censor he tried to expel Saturninus and Glaucia from the senate; in 100 he refused Saturninus' oath and went into exile until 98.
people.death: natural causes, c. 91 (rumours of poisoning)

people.name: Bocchus I
people.summary: Father-in-law of Jugurtha, he joined him against Rome in 108 for the promise of a third of Numidia, then after defeats in 106 negotiated with Sulla and handed Jugurtha over in 105, receiving western Numidia. In 91 he dedicated a gilded group of the surrender on the Capitol.
people.death: natural causes, c. 80

people.name: Scaurus
people.summary: From an impoverished patrician family, he became consul in 115 and princeps senatus for a quarter-century, the archetypal senatorial grandee, suspected of taking Jugurtha's bribes, builder of the stone Milvian Bridge and the Via Aemilia Scauri. He wrote an autobiography in three books.
people.detail: Accused in 90 of inciting the Italian allies, he answered: 'Varius of Sucro says Scaurus incited the allies to revolt; Scaurus denies it. Which of the two do you believe, citizens?', and was acquitted. Sallust depicts him as clever and corrupt; Cicero revered him.
people.death: natural causes, c. 89

people.name: Marius
people.summary: A novus homo of equestrian family from Arpinum, he married into the patrician Julii (he was Julius Caesar's uncle by marriage), won the Jugurthine War, destroyed the Cimbri and Teutones in an unprecedented run of five consecutive consulships, and was credited with recruiting the landless poor into the legions. Driven out by Sulla in 88, he returned with Cinna in 87 and died early in his seventh consulship.
people.detail: He was the first great beneficiary of the army's new dependence on its commander, but a clumsy politician: in 100 he turned on his ally Saturninus, and in 88 his greed for the Mithridatic command provoked Sulla's march on Rome. The massacres of 87 darkened his memory. Caesar restored his trophies in 65 and built his own popularity on Marius' name.
people.death: natural causes (pleurisy), 13 January 86, aged about 70
scholarship: Evans, Gaius Marius: A Political Biography (1994)
Matthew, On the Wings of Eagles (2010)

people.name: Caepio (consul 106)
people.summary: Consul in 106, he restored senatorial juries and sacked Tolosa, whose sacred treasure disappeared. His refusal to cooperate with the novus homo Mallius Maximus produced the catastrophe of Arausio (105). Stripped of command, condemned in 103 and exiled.
people.death: in exile at Smyrna, date unknown

people.name: Catulus (consul 102)
people.summary: Cultured aristocrat, poet and memoirist who shared the victory of Vercellae with Marius and disputed the credit. He vowed the round temple of Fortuna Huiusce Diei (Temple B, Largo Argentina). An enemy of Marius, he was proscribed in 87.
people.death: suicide by charcoal fumes in a freshly plastered room to avoid Marius' vengeance, 87

people.name: Boiorix
people.summary: King of the Cimbri who led them at Arausio and killed the captured legate Aurelius Scaurus; Plutarch says he rode up to the Roman camp before Vercellae to challenge Marius to fix a day and place for battle.
people.death: killed in the battle of Vercellae, 30 July 101

people.name: Saturninus
people.summary: Radical tribune and ally of Marius who passed land grants for veterans, a cheap grain law and the first law on maiestas. His use of violence, culminating in the murder of a consular candidate, led to the senatus consultum ultimum of 100 and his death in the Curia.
people.death: stoned to death with roof tiles in the Curia Hostilia, where he had been confined after surrendering, December 100

people.name: Manius Aquillius
people.summary: Marius' colleague in 101, he ended the Second Sicilian Slave War, killing Athenion in single combat. As envoy in Asia in 89 he pushed Nicomedes IV to attack Pontus, starting the First Mithridatic War.
people.death: handed to Mithridates by Mytilene and executed at Pergamon by molten gold poured down his throat, 88

people.name: Rutilius Rufus
people.summary: Stoic pupil of Panaetius, jurist and historian, he fought at the Muthul, introduced gladiatorial drill as consul after Arausio, and as Scaevola's legate in Asia protected provincials from the publicani, for which an equestrian jury convicted him of extortion in 92. He lived out his exile honoured at Smyrna.
people.death: natural causes in exile at Smyrna, after 78

people.name: Crassus the orator
people.summary: The greatest orator of his generation and Cicero's model, protagonist of the De oratore. He championed the colony at Narbo, as consul passed the lex Licinia Mucia expelling false citizens and as censor banned Latin rhetoric schools. He backed Drusus in 91.
people.death: pleurisy days after a passionate speech against the consul Philippus, September 91

people.name: Scaevola Pontifex
people.summary: Jurist who wrote the first systematic treatise on Roman civil law in 18 books, a model governor of Asia whose edict Cicero copied, and pontifex maximus. Cicero studied law with him and his cousin the augur.
people.death: murdered at the temple of Vesta on the orders of the younger Marius, 82

people.name: Marcus Livius Drusus (tribune 91)
people.summary: Son of Gaius Gracchus' opponent, he tried in 91 to reconcile everyone with a package of senatorial juries, colonies and citizenship for the Italians, and was assassinated, which triggered the Social War. His nephew Cato the Younger grew up in his house.
people.detail: Asked what he would leave his heirs, he reportedly said a house so built that all could see what he did. Dying, he asked when the Republic would again have a citizen like him.
people.death: stabbed by an unknown assassin in the atrium of his house, autumn 91

people.name: Poppaedius Silo

roles.t: Consul of the Italian confederation (Marsic group)

people.summary: Marsic leader, friend of Drusus, and the most dangerous Italian general of the Social War; Plutarch tells how, staying with Drusus, he dangled the child Cato out of a window when the boy refused to support Italian citizenship.
people.death: killed in battle against Mamercus Aemilius in Apulia, 88

people.name: Papius Mutilus

roles.t: Consul of the Italian confederation (Samnite group)

people.summary: Samnite commander of the southern Italian forces in the Social War, he overran Campania in 90 and later fought for the Marians. His coins in Oscan bear his name and the title embratur (imperator).
people.death: suicide at Teanum after his wife refused to admit him while he was proscribed, 80

sources.r: Italian allied issues with legend Mutil embratur

people.name: Pompeius Strabo
people.summary: Picene magnate and father of Pompey, he took Asculum in 89, passed the lex Pompeia giving Latin rights to the Transpadanes, and in 87 played both sides between Cinna and the senate. Hated for his greed, he died during the siege of Rome.
people.death: died in camp in 87, by lightning according to one tradition, by plague in another; the crowd dragged his body from its bier

people.name: Sulpicius
people.summary: Brilliant orator (a speaker in Cicero's De oratore) who as tribune in 88 tried to distribute the new Italian citizens across all tribes and transferred the Mithridatic command from Sulla to Marius, provoking Sulla's march on Rome.
people.death: betrayed by a slave and killed near Laurentum; his head displayed on the Rostra, 88

people.name: Sulla

roles.t: Dictator legibus scribundis et rei publicae constituendae

people.summary: Impoverished patrician who captured Jugurtha, won the Social War in the south, and as consul in 88 became the first Roman to march on Rome. He defeated Mithridates in Greece, returned to win a second civil war in 83-82, proscribed his enemies and as dictator rebuilt the constitution around a strengthened senate before retiring voluntarily.
people.detail: He called himself Felix, the Fortunate, and in Greek Epaphroditus, favoured of Aphrodite. Ancient writers saw a split personality: charming, cultivated and dissolute in youth, merciless in power. His memoirs, in 22 books, shaped later accounts. His settlement collapsed within a decade, but its institutions (standing courts, a 600-member senate, the cursus rules) lasted, and his example of a general taking the state by force haunted every later crisis.
people.death: haemorrhage at his villa near Puteoli, 78; state funeral and cremation in the Campus Martius
scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (2nd ed. 2005)
Santangelo, Sulla, the Elites and the Empire (2007)

people.name: Cinna
people.summary: Consul four years running (87-84), he championed the new Italian citizens, was driven from Rome, returned with Marius and the army from Nola, and dominated the 'Cinnanum tempus', a period of uneasy normality before Sulla's return. His daughter Cornelia married Julius Caesar.
people.death: killed by mutinous troops at Ancona while preparing to cross to Illyricum, 84

people.name: Carbo
people.summary: Leader of the Marian regime after Cinna's death, three times consul. He lost the war of 82 in the north and fled to Africa and Sicily.
people.death: captured on Cossyra and executed by Pompey at Lilybaeum, 82

people.name: Marius the Younger
people.summary: Son (perhaps adopted nephew) of Marius, elected consul at 26 in 82 for the magic of the name. Beaten by Sulla at Sacriportus, he ordered the murder of leading senators in Rome before being besieged in Praeneste.
people.death: suicide in a tunnel under Praeneste as the town surrendered, 82

people.name: Pontius Telesinus
people.summary: Samnite general who led the last Italian army against Sulla, marching on Rome itself and nearly winning at the Colline Gate, crying that the wolves must be destroyed in their lair.
people.death: killed at the battle of the Colline Gate, 1 November 82

people.name: Mithridates VI
people.fullName: Mithridates VI Eupator Dionysus, king of Pontus
people.summary: King of Pontus for 57 years and Rome's most persistent enemy, he built an empire around the Black Sea, overran Asia in 88 and ordered the massacre of the Italians there, and fought three wars against Sulla, Lucullus and Pompey. The Greek East saw him as a liberator for a time.
people.detail: Pliny says he spoke the 22 languages of his subjects; he experimented with poisons and antidotes until, the story goes, poison would not kill him. Cicero called him the greatest king after Alexander. He fought on into his late sixties, planning, it was said, to invade Italy from the north.
people.death: had his Gallic bodyguard Bituitus kill him at Panticapaeum after his son Pharnaces' revolt, 63
scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)

people.name: Archelaus
people.summary: Cappadocian Greek, Mithridates' leading general, who conquered Greece in 88, held the Piraeus against Sulla and lost the battles of Chaeronea and Orchomenus. He negotiated the preliminaries of Dardanus with Sulla; suspected of treachery by Mithridates, he went over to the Romans in 83. His son became priest-king of Comana and husband of Berenice IV.
people.death: unknown, after 83

people.name: Fimbria
people.summary: Violent Marian officer who had the consul Flaccus murdered and took over his army, beat Mithridates' son at the Rhyndacus, sacked Ilium and nearly captured Mithridates. Abandoned by his troops when Sulla arrived.
people.death: suicide in the sanctuary of Asclepius at Pergamon, 85

people.name: Metellus Pius
people.summary: Earned his cognomen Pius by campaigning for his exiled father's recall. He held out against the Marians, joined Sulla in 83, won at Faventia, and fought Sertorius for eight years in Spain, cautiously and in the end successfully. His death in 63 opened the pontificate to Caesar.
people.death: natural causes, early 63

people.name: Sertorius
people.summary: From Nursia in the Sabine hills, he fought at Arausio, spied among the Cimbri in Gallic dress, lost an eye in the Social War, and as the last Marian commander built a Romano-Iberian state in Spain that defeated Metellus and Pompey for years. He was murdered by his own officers.
people.detail: Plutarch's admiring Life (from Sallust) presents a humane, gifted commander with a counter-senate in exile, a school for Iberian nobles at Osca, and a white fawn sent by Diana; the Iberians called him a new Hannibal. Modern debate asks whether he was a Roman patriot fighting the Sullan regime or a warlord drifting into separatism.
people.death: stabbed at a banquet at Osca by Perperna and other officers, 73 or 72
scholarship: Spann, Quintus Sertorius and the Legacy of Sulla (1987)

people.name: Perperna
people.summary: Marian praetor who brought the remnant of Lepidus' army to Sertorius, resented his subordination, and murdered him. Beaten by Pompey in his first battle, he tried to buy his life with Sertorius' correspondence.
people.death: executed by Pompey, who burned Sertorius' letters unread, 72

people.name: Lepidus (consul 78)
people.summary: Enriched in the Sullan proscriptions, he turned against Sulla's system as consul in 78 and led an armed revolt in 77 that Catulus and Pompey crushed. Father of the triumvir.
people.death: died in Sardinia after his defeat, 77

people.name: Lucullus

roles.t: Quaestor (the only officer to follow Sulla to Rome)
Proquaestor and fleet commander in the East

people.summary: Sulla's most loyal officer and literary executor, he relieved Cyzicus, conquered Pontus, routed Tigranes at Tigranocerta and relieved the Asian cities of Sullan debt, but was undone by his soldiers' mutiny and the hostility of the equites, and superseded by Pompey. He spent his last years in proverbial luxury.
people.detail: Pliny credits him with bringing the cherry tree to Italy from Cerasus. His gardens on the Pincian (horti Luculliani), his fishponds at Misenum and Naples, his library open to scholars, and his banquets ('Lucullus dines with Lucullus') became bywords. Cicero made him a speaker in his Academica.
people.death: natural causes after a period of mental decline, c. 57/56

sources.w: De imperio Cn. Pompei (Pro lege Manilia)

people.name: Tigranes the Great
people.summary: Raised as a hostage at the Parthian court, he made Armenia an empire stretching to Syria, called himself King of Kings and built Tigranocerta. Son-in-law and ally of Mithridates, he was routed by Lucullus in 69 and submitted to Pompey in 66, keeping Armenia as a client kingdom.
people.death: natural causes, c. 55, aged about 85

people.name: Spartacus
people.summary: Thracian, perhaps once a soldier in Roman service, enslaved and trained as a gladiator at Capua, he led the breakout of 73 and an army of runaway slaves that defeated several Roman armies, including both consuls of 72, before Crassus crushed it in 71.
people.detail: Plutarch calls him more Hellenic than Thracian in intelligence and gentleness; Appian says he shared booty equally. There is no evidence he aimed to abolish slavery. Since Marx, who called him the finest fellow in all ancient history, he has been a modern political icon.
people.death: killed fighting in the final battle on the upper Silarus, 71; body never found
scholarship: Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)

people.name: Crixus
people.summary: Gallic gladiator who broke out of Capua with Spartacus and led the Gauls and Germans of the slave army; he separated from Spartacus and was destroyed near Mount Garganus.
people.death: killed near Mount Garganus by the praetor Arrius, 72
